lines.watchItem: Demand this cycle is named rather than forecast: one model developer's fastest inference tier runs on the leading vendor's current and next flagship parts, and one customer plans about 420,000 of that vendor's processors in a single month alongside billions of dollars of monthly capacity commitments. Leading-edge wafer-start planning is exposed to how long those named ramps hold their pace.

An independent forecaster now names availability of stacked memory, the fast memory packaged beside each accelerator, as the limit on accelerator production, while projecting that cumulative supply rises from 2.21 billion gigabytes in 2025 to 5.81 billion in 2027. Advanced-packaging allocation is exposed to a second gate one step upstream: packaging slots only convert into shipped systems when memory arrives with them.

One model lab has committed $125.2 billion over five years to custom-chip computing capacity, with its chip designer lending up to $42 billion against that lease and a bank group assembling $60 billion more for custom accelerator capacity. Leading-node customer mix is exposed to purpose-built programmes of that scale sitting next to merchant accelerator orders rather than behind them.

Published rental rates stay high, with one provider listing prior-generation capacity at $49.24 an hour and another posting $16.146 per accelerator-hour for current top-end capacity from October 7, while South Korean semiconductor exports rose 262.8 percent in September on memory price increases. Pricing power along the chain is exposed to how much of that memory cost customers keep absorbing.

Enforcement and evasion are both active: prosecutors indicted a California company over more than $300 million of restricted servers routed to China, while a state-linked Chinese finance firm funded more than 700 servers worth over $440 million, including machines using restricted top-end parts. Policy exposure sits squarely on whatever demand a China re-opening would add.

Lenders now decline chip-backed loans to small cloud operators unless the accelerator vendor posts collateral of up to 25 percent, and that vendor's $500 billion third-party capital platform had closed no transaction by early October, while one large cloud customer plans to move about $8 billion of accelerators into a separate vehicle and lease the same hardware back. The money standing behind current orders is thinner than the order totals imply.

Power now paces new sites: a ratings agency puts the requirement through 2030 at $110 billion of investment and 45 gigawatts of new generation, and a $140 billion Japanese initiative opens with a 400 megawatt campus designed to run off the public grid. Wafer-start and packaging schedules carry the exposure when sites land later than the silicon does.

A forecaster puts the spending implied by 2027 agent workloads at $2.6 trillion to $5.3 trillion a year against roughly $1 trillion of projected developer revenue by the end of that year. The demand behind today's committed capacity carries a revenue gap wide enough to show up as cancelled orders rather than as merely slower growth.
